title: Trump Threatens to Bar Bombardier From US Market as Canada Tariffs Loom, Israeli Strikes Kill 12 in Lebanon Jeopardising Ceasefire
subhead: The US-Canada trade war escalates with a direct threat to a flagship Canadian manufacturer hours before Ottawa imposes $20bn in retaliatory tariffs, while Israeli strikes in southern Lebanon kill 12 and threaten the June ceasefire. Hormuz commodity traffic falls to its lowest level since May.

sections.heading: US-Canada Trade War Escalates to a Flagship Manufacturer
sections.body:
President Donald Trump warned Canadian aircraft maker Bombardier on Monday that it can no longer sell in the United States unless it moves its manufacturing there, writing on Truth Social: 'NO MORE SELLING BOMBARDIER IN THE UNITED STATES!' The threat lands hours before Canadian retaliatory tariffs on $20bn worth of US goods are set to take effect, according to the BBC.

Bombardier, one of Canada's largest companies and a major employer in Quebec, already operates a US factory in Kansas and employs 3,500 American workers, with about half of its 5,100-aircraft fleet operated by US-based customers. Quebec premier Christine Fréchette said she would not 'respond to provocation with provocation' and that Quebec would not allow anyone to dictate where its companies must produce. Trade talks between the neighbours collapsed late last month after Canada walked away, prompting the US to impose 50% tariffs on a range of Canadian goods.
sections.whyItMatters: The dispute has moved from tariffs on goods to direct pressure on a specific flagship company, signalling a deeper rupture in the US-Canada economic relationship that underpins North American supply chains and defence-industrial cooperation.

sections.heading: Israeli Strikes in Southern Lebanon Kill 12, Threatening the June Ceasefire
sections.body:
Israeli air strikes on the village of Kfar Roummane in southern Lebanon killed at least 12 people, the Lebanese health ministry said, including two children and four women in a strike that destroyed a residential building, plus a paramedic killed in a second strike on a vehicle. The Israeli military said it struck Hezbollah infrastructure and 'several terrorists' transferring weapons, in retaliation for a drone attack on troops in an occupied area.

Lebanese President Joseph Aoun said the 'dangerous escalation' was jeopardising June's US-brokered ceasefire meant to end the conflict between Israel and Hezbollah, and urged the international community to pressure Israel to stop. Israeli attacks across southern Lebanon have killed at least 27 people over the past three days, according to the health ministry, and large numbers of residents are again fleeing areas near the Israeli-occupied 'security zone'.
sections.whyItMatters: A collapse of the US-brokered Israel-Hezbollah ceasefire would reopen a second front in the Middle East at a moment when Washington is already stretched by the war with Iran, and would further destabilise Lebanon's fragile state.

sections.heading: Hormuz Commodity Traffic Falls to Lowest Level Since May
sections.body:
An average of just 10 commodity ships transited the Strait of Hormuz daily over the past 10 days, the lowest level since May, according to data from Kpler cited by Al Jazeera. The figure marks a sharp reversal from early September, when US officials told Axios that roughly 40 vessels carrying millions of barrels of oil transited the strait on September 1 and the US Energy Secretary confirmed oil tankers moved over 17 million barrels on August 31, near pre-war levels.

Qatar warned of an 'industrial catastrophe' if the crisis continues, according to Al Jazeera's live coverage. The Institute for the Study of War notes that while US strikes have degraded some Iranian maritime surveillance and mine-laying capabilities, Iran is attempting to reconstitute the radar and naval assets needed to enforce control over the waterway, and has used shore-based rocket launchers and fast attack craft to compensate for lost radars.
sections.whyItMatters: The drop in transit shows the waterway remains contested despite US claims it is 'fully open', keeping global energy prices and shipping insurance under pressure and sustaining the economic stakes of the Iran war.

sections.heading: Ukraine's Chief Prosecutor Resigns as Corruption Scandal Threatens EU Path
sections.body:
Ukraine's chief prosecutor Ruslan Kravchenko resigned over corruption allegations linked to illegal call centres, days after anti-corruption investigators searched his offices and said they had identified a money-laundering scheme led by an official in his office. Kravchenko denied wrongdoing, saying he did not want his position used as a 'tool for political confrontation'.

The resignation comes as G7 ambassadors warned that corruption scandals could endanger Ukraine's integration into the European Union, for which it is a candidate on condition of a credible anti-corruption fight. Separately, Kyiv is enduring more daily air raid alerts than at any time since the 2022 invasion, according to BBC Verify analysis, as Russia shifts to round-the-clock strikes using faster jet-powered drones — 2,800 launched in August, almost twice July's total — that are harder to shoot down.
sections.whyItMatters: The corruption scandal tests Ukraine's EU accession credibility at a delicate moment, while Russia's new drone tactics are straining Kyiv's air defences and civilian life even as diplomatic talks over ending the war continue.

sections.heading: Serbia's Mladić Funeral Draws Thousands as EU Denounces 'Glorification'
sections.body:
Thousands turned out in Belgrade for the funeral of Ratko Mladić, the Bosnian Serb military leader convicted of genocide for his role in the 1995 Srebrenica massacre, who died aged 84 while serving a life sentence in the UN prison in The Hague. Several Serbian government ministers joined the crowds, and the funeral was led by the head of the Serbian Orthodox Church, Patriarch Porfirije.

The EU denounced the 'glorification' of Mladić, saying any glorification of war criminals, genocide denial and revisionism 'contradict the most fundamental European values and have no place in the EU or in EU candidate countries'. Serbia has been an EU candidate since 2012, though membership talks have recently stalled. A Serbian government minister had initially said Mladić would receive a state funeral, but those plans were changed after objections from European leaders.
sections.whyItMatters: The public celebration of a convicted war criminal in an EU candidate state sharpens the tension between Brussels' enlargement leverage and nationalist politics in the Western Balkans, with implications for regional stability and EU credibility.

bottomLine: Today's developments show a world juggling multiple simultaneous pressures: the US-Canada trade war has escalated from tariffs to a direct threat against a flagship manufacturer, the Israel-Hezbollah ceasefire is fraying under renewed strikes, and Hormuz traffic has fallen to its lowest since May even as Washington insists the waterway is open. Ukraine's corruption scandal and Russia's new drone tactics complicate the diplomatic track, while Serbia's public funeral for a convicted war criminal tests the EU's enlargement leverage. The common thread is fragility — of trade relationships, ceasefires, and alliances — as the international system absorbs the strain of the Iran war and its ripple effects.
